'''undivine''' (un-di-vīn′), ''a.'' Not divine; opposed to what is divine or elevated. ''Ruskin.''

'''undivorced''' (un-di-vōrst′), ''a.'' Not divorced; not separated.
{{smaller block|<poem>These died together,
Happy in ruin, ''undivorced'' by death.</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, v.}}}}

'''undivulged''' (un-di-vuljd′), ''a.'' Not divulged; not revealed or disclosed; secret. ''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 2. 52.

'''undo'''<sup>1</sup> (un-dö′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''undid'', pp. ''undone'', ppr. ''undoing''. [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''do''<sup>1</sup>.] To leave unperformed or unexecuted: usually in opposition with ''do.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>What to your wisdom seemeth best,
Do or ''undo'', as if ourself were here.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 196.}}}}

'''undo'''<sup>2</sup> (un-dö′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''undid'', pp. ''undone'', ppr. ''undoing''. [< ME. ''undon'', ''ondon'' (pret. ''undyde'', ''undede'', pp. ''undon'', ''ondon''), < AS. ''undōn'' (= OFries. ''undūa''), put back, open, undo, < ''un-'', back, + ''dōn'', put, do: see ''un-''<sup>2</sup> and ''do''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To put back into a former condition; reverse, as something which has been done; annul; bring to nought.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oute of the place swithe thei ȝede
And the tumbe thei ''vndede;''
No thing ther Inne thei ne founde,
But a manere floure at the grounde.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 98.}}
<poem>Let her not still ''undo'', with peevish Haste,
All that her Woman does.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.}}}}
'''2.''' To untie or unfasten; unloose; unfix; open.
{{smaller block|''Undo'' this button.{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. 309.}}}}

'''undoing''' (un-dö′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''undo''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The reversal of what has been done: as, there is no ''undoing'' of the past.—'''2.''' Ruin; destruction.

{{smaller block|The vtter ''vndoyng'' of some honest familie.

'''undone'''<sup>1</sup> (un-dun′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''done.''] Not done.
{{smaller block|These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other ''undone.''
{{right|Luke xi. 42.}}}}

'''undone'''<sup>2</sup> (un-dun′). Past participle of ''undo''<sup>1</sup>, ''undo''<sup>2</sup>.

'''undose''' (un′dōs), ''a.'' [< L. ''undosus,'' wavy, < ''unda,'' a wave: see ''ound, undulate.''] In ''entom.,'' wavy; undate; undulated; having undulating parallel lines.

'''undouble''' (un-dub′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''double.''] To unfold; render single.

'''undoubtable''' (un-dou′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not to be doubted; indubitable. ''Bp. Hall,'' Specialties.

'''undoubtably''' (un-dou′ta-bli), ''adv.'' Without doubt; undoubtedly. ''The Engineer,'' LXVI. 266.

'''undoubted''' (un-dou′ted), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undouted;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''doubted.''] '''1.''' Not doubted; not called in question; indubitable; indisputable.
{{smaller block|The ''undoubted'' splendour of the line of Hastings needs no illustration from fable. ''Macaulay,'' Warren Hastings.}}
'''2.''' Not filled with doubt, apprehension, fear, or the like; hence, confident; bold; fearless; redoubted.
{{smaller block|Hardy and ''undoubted'' champions.
{{right|''Shak.,'' 3 Hen. VI., v. 7. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' Not being an object of doubt or suspicion; unsuspected.
{{smaller block|<poem>More should I question thee, and more I must,
Though more to know could not be more to trust,
From whence thou camest, how tended on; but rest
Unquestion’d welcome, and ''undoubted'' blest.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' All’s Well, ii. 1. 211.}}}}

'''undress<sup>2</sup>''' (un-dres′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dress, v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To take off the clothes of; strip: as, to ''undress'' a child.
{{smaller block|Madam, ''undress'' you and come now to bed.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., Ind., l. 119.}}}}
'''2.''' To divest of ornaments or elegant attire; disrobe. ''Pope.''—'''3.''' To take the dressing, bandages, or covering from, as a wound.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take off one’s dress or clothes.
{{smaller block|To make me dress and ''undress.''
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Noble Gentleman, ii.}}}}

'''undressed''' (un-drest′), ''p. a.'' Not dressed, in any sense.

'''undrossy''' (un-dros′i), ''a.'' Not drossy; free from dross or other impurities. ''Pope.''

'''undry†''' (un-drī′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''undrien''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dry.''] To become moist.
{{smaller block|<poem>There is warme and drie,
Ablaqueate hem that thai may ''undrie.''</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 189.}}}}

'''undubitable†''' (un-dū′bi-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Indubitable. ''Locke.''

'''undue''' (un-dū′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not due; not yet demandable by right; not yet owing: as, a debt, note, or bond ''undue.''—'''2.''' Not right; not lawful; improper; unworthy: as, an ''undue'' proceeding.
{{smaller block|Having first try’d in vaine all ''undue'' ways to procure Mony, . . . upon meer extremitie he summond this last Parlament.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, i.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''3.''' Erring by excess; excessive; inordinate; disproportioned: as, an ''undue'' regard to the externals of religion; an ''undue'' attachment to forms; an ''undue'' rigor in the execution of law.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pleasure admitted in ''undue'' degree
Enslaves the will, nor leaves the judgment free.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Progress of Error, l. 269.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Undue influence''', that control which one obtains over another whereby the latter is made to do in important affairs what of his free will he would not do. It differs wholly from ''persuasion'', in which falsehood does not mingle, for that merely leads the will, while undue influence coerces it. (''Cooley.'') The undue influence which renders void a will procured by it is such as imposes a restraint on the will of the testator, so that the act represents not his will, but the will of another.}}

'''undueness''' (un-dū′nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being undue. ''Roget.'' [Rare.]

'''unduke''' (un-dūk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''duke.''] To deprive of the rank of duke.
{{smaller block|He hath letters from France that the King hath ''unduked'' twelve Dukes.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Dec. 12, 1663.}}}}

'''undulant''' (un′dū-lant), ''a.'' [= F. ''ondulant'' = Sp. ''ondulante'', < NL. *''undulan(t-)s'', ppr. of *''undulare'', undulate: see ''undulate.''] Undulating; undulatory.
{{smaller block|<poem>And on her deck sea-spirits I descried
Gliding and lapsing in an ''undulant'' dance.</poem>
{{right|''Taylor'', St. Clement’s Eve, ii. 2. (''Davies.'')}}
<poem>Naked arms
More white and ''undulant'' than necks of swans.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Parting of the Ways.}}}}

'''undulary†''' (un′dū-lā-ri), ''a.'' [< L. *''undula'', dim. of ''unda'', wave (see ''undulate''), + ''-ary.''] Undulating.

''undōn'' (= OFries. ''undūa''), put back, open, undo, < ''un-'', back, + ''dōn'', put, do: see ''un-''<sup>2</sup> and ''do''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To put back into a former condition; reverse, as something which has been done; annul; bring to nought.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oute of the place swithe thei ȝede

'''2.''' To untie or unfasten; unloose; unfix; open.
{{smaller block|''Undo'' this button.{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. 309.}}}}

{{smaller block|A knife, a knife, I say!—O, Master Allum, if you love a woman, draw out your knife, and ''undo'' me [cut her stay lace], ''undo'' me! ''Webster and Dekker'', Northward Ho, ii. 1.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But, at the Prioress’ command,
A monk ''undid'' the silken band
That tied her tresses fair.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, ii. 20.}}}}
'''3.''' To find the answer or explanation of; solve. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Pray you, ''undo'' this riddle,
And tell me how I have vex’d you?</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', False One, iv. 2.}}}}
'''4.''' To bring ruin or distress upon; ruin the morals, character, reputation, or prospects of; destroy; annihilate; spoil; ruin.
{{smaller block|This love will ''undo'' us all. ''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 1. 120.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fool that I am! I have ''undone'' myself,
And with my own hand turn’d my fortune round,
That was a fair one.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Twas I betray’d your sister, I ''undid'' her.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Wretch by Fortune or by Love ''undone!''</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', To Sleep.}}}}
'''5†.''' To reveal; disclose; unfold; explain.
{{smaller block|<poem>Me lakketh bothe English and wit
For to ''undo'' hit at the fulle.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 899.}}}}
'''6†.''' To be too much for the power of; baffle.
{{smaller block|Which lames report to follow it and ''undoes'' description to do it. ''Shak.'', W. T., v. 2. 63.}}

'''undock''' (un-dok′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dock''<sup>3</sup>.] To take out of dock: as, to dock and ''undock'' a ship.

'''undoctor''' (un-dok′tọr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''doctor''.] To divest (one’s self) of the character of a doctor. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|My brother-in-law is a paragon of the class [physicians], but he is so by — in as much as possible — ''undoctoring'' himself.
{{right|''Carlyle'', in Froude, II.}}}}

'''undoer''' (un-dö′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''undo''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who undoes, in any sense; one who reverses what has been done; one who ruins. ''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 12.

{{smaller block|And be mine own ''undoer''. ''Heywood'', English Traveller.}}

'''undoing''' (un-dö′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''undo''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The reversal of what has been done: as, there is no ''undoing'' of the past.—'''2.''' Ruin; destruction.

{{smaller block|The vtter ''vndoyng'' of some honest familie.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 242.}}}}
<poem>Of havoc tired and rash ''undoing'',
Man left this Structure to become Time’s prey.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Sonnets, iii. 47.}}}}

'''undomesticate''' (un-dọ̄-mes′ti-kāt), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To estrange from home life or duties. ''Richardson'', Grandison, ii. 11.—'''2.''' To make wild or roving; untame: as, to ''undomesticate'' an animal. [Rare.]

'''undomesticated''' (un-dọ̄-mes′ti-kā-ted), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Not domesticated; not accustomed to a family life.—'''2.''' Not tamed, as an animal.

'''undomestication''' (un-dọ̄-mes-ti-kā′shọn), ''n.'' The act or process of making wild, as an animal, Evolution of Morbid Germs, iv. 60. [Rare.]

'''undone'''<sup>1</sup> (un-dun′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''done.''] Not done.
{{smaller block|These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other ''undone.''
{{right|Luke xi. 42.}}}}

'''undone'''<sup>2</sup> (un-dun′). Past participle of ''undo''<sup>1</sup>, ''undo''<sup>2</sup>.

'''undose''' (un′dōs), ''a.'' [< L. ''undosus,'' wavy, < ''unda,'' a wave: see ''ound, undulate.''] In ''entom.,'' wavy; undate; undulated; having undulating parallel lines.

'''undouble''' (un-dub′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''double.''] To unfold; render single.

'''undoubtable''' (un-dou′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not to be doubted; indubitable. ''Bp. Hall,'' Specialties.

'''undoubtably''' (un-dou′ta-bli), ''adv.'' Without doubt; undoubtedly. ''The Engineer,'' LXVI. 266.

'''undoubted''' (un-dou′ted), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undouted;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''doubted.''] '''1.''' Not doubted; not called in question; indubitable; indisputable.
{{smaller block|The ''undoubted'' splendour of the line of Hastings needs no illustration from fable. ''Macaulay,'' Warren Hastings.}}
'''2.''' Not filled with doubt, apprehension, fear, or the like; hence, confident; bold; fearless; redoubted.
{{smaller block|Hardy and ''undoubted'' champions.
{{right|''Shak.,'' 3 Hen. VI., v. 7. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' Not being an object of doubt or suspicion; unsuspected.
{{smaller block|<poem>More should I question thee, and more I must,
Though more to know could not be more to trust,
From whence thou camest, how tended on; but rest
Unquestion’d welcome, and ''undoubted'' blest.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' All’s Well, ii. 1. 211.}}}}

'''undoubted†''' (un-dou′ted), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''undouted, undowted''; < ''undoubted'', ''a.''] Undoubtedly.

{{smaller block|And ''vndowted'' this lytell Chapell of the byrthe of our Lorde is the most glorious and deuoute place that euer I come in. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 37.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Undoubted'' it were moche better to be occupyed in honest recreation than to do nothyng. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 26.}}}}

'''undoubtedly''' (un-dou′ted-li), ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. ''undowghtedly''; < ''undoubted'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Without doubt; without question; indubitably.

{{smaller block|''Undowghtedly'' in a prince . . . may be nothinge more excellent . . . than to aduaunce men after the estimation of their goodnes. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 13.}}}}

'''undoubtful''' (un-dout′fu̇l), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not doubtful; not ambiguous; plain; evident.

{{smaller block|His fact . . . came not to an ''undoubtful'' proof. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 2. 142.}}}}

'''2.''' Harboring no doubt or suspicion; unsuspicious.

<poem>Our husbands might have looked into our thoughts
And made themselves ''undoubtful.''</poem>{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune.}}

'''undoubting''' (un-dou′ting), ''a.'' Not doubting; not hesitating respecting facts; not fluctuating in uncertainty: as, an ''undoubting'' believer; an ''undoubting'' faith.

{{smaller block|They are captivated into a confident and ''undoubting'' persuasion that they are savingly wrought upon. {{right|''J. Edwards'', Works, III. 27.}}}}

'''undoubtingly''' (un-dou′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an undoubting manner; without doubting; certainly.

{{smaller block|We know ''undoubtingly'' what good is, and what evil is. {{right|''H. S. Holland'', Logic and Life, p. 62.}}}}

'''undoubtous†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''undoutous'', ''undowtous''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''doubtous.''] Undoubting; certain.
{{smaller block|''Undowtous'' feyth. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 1.}}}}

'''undrainable''' (un-drā′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being drained or exhausted; inexhaustible.
{{smaller block|Mine ''undrainable'' of ore. {{right|''Tennyson'', Œnone.}}}}

'''undrape''' (un-drāp′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''drape.''] To strip of drapery; uncover.

'''undraped''' (un-drāpt′), ''a.'' Not draped; not arranged in folds pleasing to the eye, or so as to hang artistically; also, not covered with drapery; not clothed; nude: as, an ''undraped'' statue.

'''undraw''' (un-drâ′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''undrew'', pp. ''undrawn'', ppr. ''undrawing.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''draw.''] To draw aside or open.
{{smaller block|Angels ''undrew'' the curtains of the throne. {{right|''Young.''}}}}

'''undrawn''' (un-drân′), ''a.'' Not drawn. {{smaller|(''a'') Not pulled, dragged, or hauled.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Forth rushed with whirlwind sound
The chariot of paternal Deity,
Flashing thick flames, wheel within wheel, ''undrawn'',
Itself instinct with spirit.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 751.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not portrayed or delineated.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The deathbed of the just is yet ''undrawn''
By mortal hand.</poem>{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Not drawn, as from a cask. Your holy reverence for the Sabbath-day.
{{right|''Byron'', English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.}}}}

'''undreaded''' (un-dred′ed), ''a.'' Not dreaded; not feared.
{{smaller block|Unnamed, ''undreaded'', and thyself half-starved.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 595.}}}}

'''undreamed, undreamt''' (un-drēmd′, un-dremt′), ''a.'' Not dreamed; not thought of; not imagined: often followed by ''of''.
{{smaller block|Many things fall out by the design of the general motor, and ''undreamt of'' contrivance of nature.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iii. 10.}}
Unpath’d waters, ''undream’d'' shores.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 578.}}}}

'''undreaming''' (un-drē′ming), ''a.'' Not dreaming; unmindful: with ''of''.
{{smaller block|The days when, ''undreaming of'' Theatres and Managerships, thou wert a scholar, and an early ripe one, under the roofs builded by the munificent and pious Colet.
{{right|''Lamb'', Elia (1877), p. 295.}}}}

'''undress'''<sup>1</sup> (un-dres′ or un′dres), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dress'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' Ordinary dress, as opposed to full dress or uniform, regarded as “dress” in a special sense; a loose negligent dress.
{{smaller block|The Queen came to Lady Bathurst’s to see the review, and held a sort of drawing-room; . . . everybody was in ''undress'' except the officers. {{right|''Greville'', Memoirs, July 20, 1830.}}
I am a woman of quality . . . for all I am in an ''undress'' this morning. {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Provoked Wife, iv. 3.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to ordinary attire; hence, informal; unostentatious; simple: as, an ''undress'' uniform.
{{smaller block|His ''undress'' life (if we may use the phrase). {{right|''Swift.''}}}} '''Undress guard-mounting.''' {{smaller|See ''parade guard-mounting,'' under ''parade.''}}—'''Undress parade.''' {{smaller|See ''parade.''}}

{{smaller block|To make me dress and ''undress.''

'''undrossy''' (un-dros′i), ''a.'' Not drossy; free from dross or other impurities. ''Pope.''

{{smaller block|<poem>There is warme and drie,
Ablaqueate hem that thai may ''undrie.''</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 189.}}}}

'''undubitable†''' (un-dū′bi-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Indubitable. ''Locke.''

'''undue''' (un-dū′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not due; not yet demandable by right; not yet owing: as, a debt, note, or bond ''undue.''—'''2.''' Not right; not lawful; improper; unworthy: as, an ''undue'' proceeding.
{{smaller block|Having first try’d in vaine all ''undue'' ways to procure Mony, . . . upon meer extremitie he summond this last Parlament.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, i.}}}}

'''3.''' Erring by excess; excessive; inordinate; disproportioned: as, an ''undue'' regard to the externals of religion; an ''undue'' attachment to forms; an ''undue'' rigor in the execution of law.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pleasure admitted in ''undue'' degree
Enslaves the will, nor leaves the judgment free.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Progress of Error, l. 269.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Undue influence''', that control which one obtains over another whereby the latter is made to do in important affairs what of his free will he would not do. It differs wholly from ''persuasion'', in which falsehood does not mingle, for that merely leads the will, while undue influence coerces it. (''Cooley.'') The undue influence which renders void a will procured by it is such as imposes a restraint on the will of the testator, so that the act represents not his will, but the will of another.}}

'''undueness''' (un-dū′nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being undue. ''Roget.'' [Rare.]

'''unduke''' (un-dūk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''duke.''] To deprive of the rank of duke.
{{smaller block|He hath letters from France that the King hath ''unduked'' twelve Dukes.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Dec. 12, 1663.}}}}

'''undulant''' (un′dū-lant), ''a.'' [= F. ''ondulant'' = Sp. ''ondulante'', < NL. *''undulan(t-)s'', ppr. of *''undulare'', undulate: see ''undulate.''] Undulating; undulatory.
{{smaller block|<poem>And on her deck sea-spirits I descried
Gliding and lapsing in an ''undulant'' dance.</poem>
{{right|''Taylor'', St. Clement’s Eve, ii. 2. (''Davies.'')}}
<poem>Naked arms
More white and ''undulant'' than necks of swans.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Parting of the Ways.}}}}

'''undulary†''' (un′dū-lā-ri), ''a.'' [< L. *''undula'', dim. of ''unda'', wave (see ''undulate''), + ''-ary.''] Undulating.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
